A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RepetitionCurse, with matching authors and the same central attack. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–E were included in the comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original routing measurements, local and commercial-API latency experiments, prompt robustness tests, and simulated defensive expert placement.

after.justification: V2 reports original mixed-batch latency experiments, routing analyses, commercial-API measurements, workload-distribution fits, perplexity measurements, and dynamic EPLB evaluations.

M1.justification: The attack still repeats identical tokens outside the instruction template and system prompt. The capacity-constrained greedy expert-placement algorithm is also unchanged between v1 Algorithm 1 and v2 Appendix C. V2's embedding-variance objective formalizes the existing attack without introducing an optimization procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds ShareGPT conversational workloads, BurstGPT request traces, and SWE-bench code patches. Evaluation now includes mixed benign/adversarial batches and attack-adapted EPLB environments. Conversely, v1's backend-architecture identification scenario is removed. These substantially change the represented traffic and test scenarios.

E2.justification: V1 compares vulnerability-aware placement with the default expert mapping. V2 Appendix E/Table 7 adds EPLB-derived mappings, learned from benign-only and attack-mixed traffic, as evaluated comparators against the same static placement algorithm. This is a focused expansion of the defense comparator set.

E3.justification: Local latency evaluation changes from 200 attack and 200 normal prompts of 20,000 tokens to 2,048 requests of 1,000–5,000 tokens, packed into 16,384-token batches with controlled attack fractions. V2 extends supported deployments to EP sizes 16 and 32 and defines kernel LAR using summed layer times. The model panel removes two Qwen3-Next variants and adds Kimi-Linear-Base.

E4.justification: V2 adds attack-fraction and adaptive-EPLB analyses, workload-dependent SLA projections, and computation-time decomposition. It expands the earlier perplexity observation into a comparison across lengths and natural/code inputs, and augments expert-vulnerability analysis with effective expert counts. V1's side-channel analysis is removed; the length/context robustness analysis is retained.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix B adds statistical fitting of lognormal distributions to BurstGPT and ShareGPT request lengths and uses estimated shape parameters to project SLA compliance. Both versions already report 95% lower confidence bounds for API LAR and display entropy error bars. No increase in repeated runs or seed counts is documented.

E6.justification: V1 Table 3 reports Mixtral-8x7B EP8 kernel LAR of 2.651; under the revised batch protocol, v2 Table 2 reports 2.01/2.68 for half/full attack batches and TTFT LARs of 1.61/2.48. These are results under different conditions. New SLA, perplexity, and EPLB results are added. Eight retained commercial-API rows keep their values, while eight other rows are removed.

T1.justification: V2 introduces formal hidden-state dispersion and an associated optimization objective in Equations 3–4, plus an effective-expert-count definition in Equation 8. Appendix B adds lognormal latency assumptions and derives the change in SLA compliance under multiplicative slowdown. The earlier theoretical maximum imbalance and bottleneck formulas are retained.

C1.justification: V2 removes backend-architecture inference as a claimed contribution and replaces it with systematic measurement of serving impact. The abstract shifts from the 3.063× commercial-API headline to 20%–148% TTFT increases on eight-GPU deployments. The introduction adds quantified SLA-violation claims and explicitly claims the first demonstration of routing imbalance weaponized for DoS.

C2.justification: V1 presents perplexity filtering as a potential defense; v2 Appendix D calls it impractical because of legitimate low-perplexity code and screening overhead. V2 emphasizes placement-defense failure at high EP or small top-k, limited EPLB adaptation, and workload-dependent SLA consequences. V1's fallback-expert hypothesis and backend-identification interpretations are dropped.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies A800 hardware and node configurations, system-prompt lengths, minute-spaced API requests, and Llama-3-8B as the perplexity evaluator. Appendix A clarifies exclusion of quantized models from the survey. Conversely, v1's explicit 20,000-token truncation for the LongBench routing illustration is no longer specified.

R1.justification: V2 reframes the prior-art comparison around compute inefficiency per input token versus resource exhaustion through generated tokens or tool calls, alongside an explicit first-routing-DoS claim. It adds CRABS, Zhou et al. (2026), capacity-aware inference, and SLO-serving literature, while removing the privacy/cache-leakage strand associated with v1's side-channel contribution.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten. Related Work moves before Background, which gains an SLO/SLA subsection, and experiments are reorganized around three research questions with explicit answers. Survey details and the placement algorithm move into appendices, while defense discussion is redistributed across the main text and appendices.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the compact kernel-latency table with a full-width table combining kernel and TTFT measurements across attack fractions and EP sizes. Vulnerability heatmaps are redesigned with effective-expert profiles. The prompt illustration is removed; a batch-timing diagram, workload plots, and three appendix result tables are added. Existing survey and algorithm displays are relocated.

improvement.justification: Controlled mixed-user batches, larger deployments, and adaptive EPLB tests address important gaps in v1's evidence for practical serving impact and defense resilience. Clearer setup documentation and removal of latency-only backend-identification claims strengthen the paper. Commercial-API coverage is reduced, SLA percentages depend on lognormal projections, and the claimed filtering false positives are not directly measured. These limitations temper but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence for the central DoS claim.
